key_insight: Medical adaptation reshaped rather than reduced aggregate risk-bearing language, which was not significantly associated with factual hallucination rates.
clinical_relevance: Patient-facing medical AI evaluation should assess potentially harmful language alongside factual accuracy.
method: Evaluated six general and medically adapted instruction-tuned models on 200 real patient questions from K-QA.
Scored six categories of risk-bearing language using a clinical-harm-informed rubric.
Used a three-judge LLM ensemble to classify severity and compared adaptation-specific risk patterns.
evidence_signal: Risk-bearing language and hallucination rates showed little association (pooled Spearman ρ = −0.065; n = 300; 95% CI −0.18 to 0.05), while category-level judge agreement varied substantially (Krippendorff α = 0.19–0.71).
watch_item: Low judge agreement in clinical-judgment-dependent categories limits automated evaluation reliability; these language-based scores do not establish actual patient harm.
paper_title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
